claim: The Virtual Burrow Assay measures approach and avoidance behaviors in head-fixed mice at millisecond timescale.
source: We have designed an assay that measures approach and avoidance behaviors in head-fixed mice at millisecond timescale, is compatible with standard electrophysiological and optical methods for measuring neuronal activity, and requires no training.
evidence: The abstract directly states this as a key feature of the assay, and subsequent figures (e.g., Figure 2B showing millisecond-scale ingress responses) provide supporting data.

claim: The Virtual Burrow Assay is compatible with standard electrophysiological and optical methods for measuring neuronal activity.
source: We have designed an assay that measures approach and avoidance behaviors in head-fixed mice at millisecond timescale, is compatible with standard electrophysiological and optical methods for measuring neuronal activity, and requires no training.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates electrophysiological recording in Figure 7 and mentions 2-photon calcium imaging through GRIN lens in the Discussion.

claim: The Virtual Burrow Assay requires no training.
source: We have designed an assay that measures approach and avoidance behaviors in head-fixed mice at millisecond timescale, is compatible with standard electrophysiological and optical methods for measuring neuronal activity, and requires no training.
evidence: Multiple experiments throughout the manuscript demonstrate immediate behavioral responses without prior training, as shown in Figures 1C, 2B, and described in the Results section.

claim: The Virtual Burrow Assay provides a sensitive readout of habituation, discrimination and exploration, as well as avoidance of both conditioned and innately aversive cues.
source: The assay provides a sensitive readout of habituation, discrimination and exploration, as well as avoidance of both conditioned and innately aversive cues.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates habituation (Figure 4), discrimination (Figure 4), exploration (Figure 4E-H), innate avoidance (Figures 2-3), and conditioned avoidance (Figure 5).

claim: Mice in the wild must balance the need to seek safety inside their burrow with the need to gather information and resources in the outside world.
source: Mice in the wild must balance the need to seek safety inside their burrow with the need to gather information and resources in the outside world (Birke et al., 1985; Blanchard and Blanchard, 2008; Blanchard and Blanchard, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on mouse behavior.

claim: Behavioral assays for head-fixed mice typically require several sessions of acclimation to head-fixation and task training.
source: Behavioral assays for head-fixed mice typically require several sessions of acclimation to head-fixation and task training, even for relatively simple applications such as measuring sensory discrimination (Guo et al., 2014) or obtaining controlled locomotion in a visual (Dombeck et al., 2010), or olfactory (Radvansky and Dombeck, 2018) virtual-reality environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies describing training requirements for head-fixed behavioral assays.

claim: When placed in the virtual burrow mice retreat inside the enclosure, pulling the tube up around their bodies as far as possible.
source: When placed in the virtual burrow mice retreat inside the enclosure, pulling the tube up around their bodies as far as possible—a behavior we have termed 'ingress' (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This behavior is demonstrated in Figure 1C showing tube position over time, and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: All mice tested exhibit ingress behavior immediately after being introduced into the VBA.
source: All mice we have tested exhibit this behavior immediately after being introduced into the VBA, remaining fully inside the virtual burrow with only transient excursions from the ingress position (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows data from N=10 mice all exhibiting this behavior, with histogram showing distribution of tube position.

claim: Neither training nor acclimation to the assay is required to observe consistent and sustained ingress.
source: Neither training nor acclimation to the assay is required to observe this consistent and sustained ingress.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates immediate ingress behavior in naive mice across multiple experiments (Figures 1C, 2B, etc.).

claim: When the enclosure is retracted by a motor, mice invariably try to get back inside.
source: When the enclosure is retracted by a motor tethered to the virtual burrow, mice invariably try to get back inside (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Figure 1D shows force measurements demonstrating resistance to retraction across N=10 mice.

claim: Mice generate between 0.4 and 1 N of force when resisting retraction of the virtual burrow.
source: This effort typically generates between 0.4 and 1 N of force, corresponding in some cases to more than three times animal's own body weight (in grams-force).
evidence: Figure 1D shows force measurements with inset histogram showing distribution of total force exerted.

claim: Mice quickly adapt to the retraction scenario, exhibiting within one to three minutes periods of >15 s during which they voluntarily hold the virtual burrow in the egress position.
source: After an initial bout of resistance (<30 s), mice voluntarily maintain an 'egress' position and thus can be presented test stimuli. Mice quickly adapt to this scenario, exhibiting within one to three minutes periods of >15 s during which they voluntarily hold the virtual burrow in the egress position.
evidence: This is described in the Results section and demonstrated across multiple experimental paradigms in subsequent figures.

claim: The sequence of ingress and resistance behaviors has been observed in all mice tested.
source: This sequence of behaviors has been observed in all mice tested and been found to persist across repeated tests on four separate days over a 16 day interval (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows data from N=5 mice tested on four separate days with no significant differences.

claim: No prior acclimation to handling or head fixation is required for mice to exhibit ingress and resistance behaviors in the VBA.
source: No prior acclimation to handling or head fixation is required.
evidence: This is stated explicitly and demonstrated by the immediate behavioral responses observed in naive mice throughout the manuscript.

claim: Strong air puffs delivered to the snout (80 psi, 2 mm distance) elicited short-latency, rapid ingress in all mice tested on all trials.
source: Strong air puffs delivered to the snout (80 psi, 2 mm distance) elicited short-latency, rapid ingress in all mice tested on all trials (Figure 2B; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Figure 2B shows 15 ingress responses from a single animal, and the text reports data from N=5 mice with 3 trials each.

claim: The latency of ingress to strong air puff varied little across animals (μ = 18.5 msec, cv = 0.07, N = 5 mice, three trials per mouse).
source: The latency of ingress varied little across animals (μ = 18.5 msec, cv = 0.07, N = 5 mice, three trials per mouse) and across trials (cv = 0.10).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported from the air puff experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Weak air puffs (2 psi, 15 cm distance) did not elicit ingress but instead a transient movement resulting in no net change in burrow position.
source: Weak air puffs (2 psi, 15 cm distance) did not elicit ingress but instead a transient movement resulting in no net change in burrow position.
evidence: Figure 2C shows an example of this flinch-like response to weak air puff.

claim: The flinch-like startle response to weak air puff can be clearly distinguished from the ongoing movement of the burrow caused by the animal's breathing.
source: This apparent flinch-like startle response (Davis, 1984) can be clearly distinguished from the ongoing movement of the burrow caused by the animal's breathing (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows the breathing oscillations and the distinct flinch response.

claim: Mice ingressed on all trials when air puffs were directed at the snout (N = 4 mice, three trials each).
source: As observed previously, all animals ingressed on all trials when air puffs were directed at the snout (Figure 2E orange and 2F left, N = 4 mice, three trials each).
evidence: Figure 2E and 2F show the data for air puffs directed at the snout in the tube configuration.

claim: Mice invariably ingressed when air puffs were directed at the hindquarters (N = 4 mice, three trials each).
source: When air puffs were directed at the hindquarters, mice also invariably ingressed (Figure 2E green and 2F second from left, N = 4 mice, three trials each).
evidence: Figure 2E and 2F show the data for air puffs directed at the hindquarters in the tube configuration.

claim: The drive to ingress into the virtual burrow overcomes the drive to move in the direction opposite the air puff.
source: Thus the drive to ingress into the virtual burrow overcomes the drive to move in the direction opposite the air puff.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mice ingress regardless of whether air puffs are directed at the snout or hindquarters (Figure 2E, F).

claim: Mice on a flat, open platform exhibited a transient, flinch-like response to air puff with little net preference between the egress or ingress directions.
source: Mice in this configuration exhibited a transient, flinch-like response to air puff delivered to the snout or hindquarters (N = 4 mice each, three trials each) followed, in some cases, by relatively small displacements of the platform with little net preference between the egress or ingress directions (Figure 2E pink and blue, 2F second from right and right, median displacement of 14.9 mm and 17.0 mm in tube vs. 0.2 mm and 2.3 mm on platform, for snout and hindquarters, respectively).
evidence: Figure 2E and 2F show the platform data compared to tube data, demonstrating the difference in response.

claim: Ingress to air puff in the VBA reflects an innate behavioral program to flee to shelter.
source: These observations, together with the stereotypy, high reproducibility across animals, and low latency of the response to strong air puff, and the fact that these behaviors require no training, suggest that ingress to air puff in the VBA reflects an innate behavioral program to flee to shelter.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple observations including stereotypy, reproducibility, low latency, lack of training requirement, and the comparison between tube and platform configurations.

claim: Mice in the VBA ingressed on 80% of trials in response to an expanding black disk displayed above their heads.
source: Mice in the VBA ingressed on 80% of trials in response to an expanding black disk displayed above their heads (Figure 3A, top left, B, top, C, orange, and D, left; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Figure 3B, C, and D show the responses to the looming stimulus across N=3 mice with 5 trials each.

claim: The habituation to repeated looming stimulation reported in freely moving mice was not observed in the VBA.
source: The habituation to repeated stimulation reported in freely moving mice (De Franceschi et al., 2016) was not observed in the VBA (Figure 3B, top).
evidence: Figure 3B shows consistent responses across trials without habituation, contrasting with cited literature on freely moving mice.

claim: A contracting black disk elicited ingress on 0% of trials.
source: These stimuli did not reliably elicit ingress, yielding responses on 0% or 13% of trials, respectively (Figure 3B, middle and bottom, C, pink and green, D, middle and right).
evidence: Figure 3B, C, and D show the responses to the receding stimulus across N=3 mice with 5 trials each.

claim: A small black disk sweeping across the visual field elicited ingress on 13% of trials.
source: These stimuli did not reliably elicit ingress, yielding responses on 0% or 13% of trials, respectively (Figure 3B, middle and bottom, C, pink and green, D, middle and right).
evidence: Figure 3B, C, and D show the responses to the sweeping stimulus across N=3 mice with 5 trials each.

claim: A visual stimulus that elicits flight in freely moving mice elicits ingress in the VBA.
source: These data show that a visual stimulus that elicits flight in freely moving mice elicits ingress in the VBA and that control stimuli that do not elicit flight do not elicit ingress.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the looming stimulus (which elicits flight in freely moving mice per De Franceschi et al., 2016) with control stimuli in the VBA.

claim: Control visual stimuli that do not elicit flight in freely moving mice do not elicit ingress in the VBA.
source: These data show that a visual stimulus that elicits flight in freely moving mice elicits ingress in the VBA and that control stimuli that do not elicit flight do not elicit ingress.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the receding and sweeping stimuli not eliciting ingress in the VBA, consistent with their lack of flight-inducing properties in freely moving mice.

claim: Mice reliably ingress to initial presentations of an odorant stimulus.
source: We observed that mice reliably ingress to initial presentations of an odorant stimulus, and their response decreases over the course of repeated stimulation (ingress on 67% of first three trials; 10% of subsequent trials, N = 5 mice, Figure 4B, left, Figure 4C, orange, and Figure 4D, left).
evidence: Figure 4B, C, and D show the habituation data for Odor 1 across N=5 mice.

claim: The ingress response to odorants decreases over the course of repeated stimulation (ingress on 67% of first three trials; 10% of subsequent trials).
source: We observed that mice reliably ingress to initial presentations of an odorant stimulus, and their response decreases over the course of repeated stimulation (ingress on 67% of first three trials; 10% of subsequent trials, N = 5 mice, Figure 4B, left, Figure 4C, orange, and Figure 4D, left).
evidence: Figure 4B, C, and D show the habituation data demonstrating decreased responses over trials.

claim: The ingress response to odorants is odor-selective.
source: This response is odor-selective: after 15 presentations of the first odorant (Odor 1) we randomly interleaved it with a second odorant (Odor 2) and observed that animals selectively ingressed to the second, but remained habituated to the first odor (ingress on 47% of first three Odor 2 trials; 12% of subsequent trials, Figure 4B,C blocks 16–30, and Figure 4D, middle).
evidence: Figure 4B, C, and D show selective responses to novel odors while remaining habituated to familiar ones.

claim: Animals selectively ingressed to a third novel odorant after habituation to the first two (ingress on 60% of first three Odor 3 trials; 8% of subsequent trials).
source: After 15 further blocks of Odor 1 and Odor 2, resulting in habituation to the second odor, we randomly interleaved them with a third odorant (Odor 3), and once again observed selective ingress to the new odor (ingress on 60% of first three Odor 3 trials; 8% of subsequent trials, Figure 4B,C blocks 31–45, and Figure 4D, right).
evidence: Figure 4B, C, and D show selective responses to the third novel odor.

claim: The selective response to a second odor following habituation to the first demonstrates that the response decrement is due neither to adaptation of the sensory epithelium nor to effector fatigue.
source: The selective response to a second odor following habituation to the first (Figure 4B–D) demonstrates that the response decrement is due neither to adaptation of the sensory epithelium nor to effector fatigue (Groves and Thompson, 1970; Rankin et al., 2009; Thompson and Spencer, 1966).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that mice respond to novel odors while remaining habituated to familiar ones, ruling out sensory or motor fatigue.

claim: Mice exited the virtual burrow for brief (~1 s) bouts before resuming a fully ingressed position when the odor source was coupled to the burrow.
source: We observed that under this configuration mice exited the virtual burrow for brief (~1 s) bouts before resuming a fully ingressed position (Figure 4F, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Figure 4F and 4G show examples of egress bouts in response to odor when the odor port is coupled to the burrow.

claim: The egress response to odor habituated, with animals egressing further on earlier than on later trials (median egress 21.9 mm for trials 1–2 vs. 10.5 mm for trials 3–5, N = 5 mice).
source: This response habituated, with the animals egressing further on earlier than on later trials (median egress 21.9 mm for trials 1–2 vs. 10.5 mm for trials 3–5, N = 5 mice, Figure 4G,H).
evidence: Figure 4G and 4H show the habituation of egress responses across trials.

claim: The VBA measures selective responses to unanticipated stimuli—ingress or egress, depending upon the configuration of the assay.
source: Together, these results indicate that the VBA measures selective responses to unanticipated stimuli—ingress or egress, depending upon the configuration of the assay—and that these behaviors can be employed to measure habituation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the habituation experiments showing both ingress (Figure 4A-D) and egress (Figure 4E-H) responses.

claim: After odor-shock conditioning, mice continued to ingress to the CS+ with greater ingress likelihood (CS+ 72%, CS- 26%, Odor3 33%, mean across trials 2–7).
source: However, they continued to ingress to the CS+, exhibiting both a greater ingress likelihood (CS+ 72%, CS- 26%, Odor3 33%, mean across trials 2–7, six trials per mouse, pooled across N = 9 mice) as well as a greater displacement (median ingress 9.98 mm for CS+, 0.27 mm for CS-, and 0.36 mm for Odor3, N = 9 mice, Figure 5B,C,E,G,I) in response to the CS+ than to the CS- or Odor3.
evidence: Figure 5 shows the conditioning data with statistical analysis demonstrating selective responses to CS+.

claim: After odor-shock conditioning, mice exhibited greater displacement in response to CS+ (median ingress 9.98 mm) than to CS- (0.27 mm) or Odor3 (0.36 mm).
source: However, they continued to ingress to the CS+, exhibiting both a greater ingress likelihood (CS+ 72%, CS- 26%, Odor3 33%, mean across trials 2–7, six trials per mouse, pooled across N = 9 mice) as well as a greater displacement (median ingress 9.98 mm for CS+, 0.27 mm for CS-, and 0.36 mm for Odor3, N = 9 mice, Figure 5B,C,E,G,I) in response to the CS+ than to the CS- or Odor3.
evidence: Figure 5I shows the distribution of maximum change in burrow position for each condition during Test.

claim: A high frequency oscillatory response (trembling) was observed in response to CS+ following conditioning.
source: On occasion we noted a second behavioral response evoked by the CS+ following conditioning: an oscillation in burrow position (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows examples of the oscillatory response during CS+ presentation.

claim: The high frequency oscillatory response was associated with trembling of the animal's body.
source: Simultaneous video recording (not shown) indicated that this high frequency oscillatory response was associated with trembling of the animal's body.
evidence: This is stated based on video observations, though the video itself is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Trembling was selective for the CS+ following conditioning.
source: While we observed ingress without trembling, on some trials trembling preceded ingress by several seconds (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, top trace), or occurred on ingress-free trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, middle trace), and was selective for the CS+ following conditioning.
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows trembling responses only during CS+ trials.

claim: The median latency to ingress to the CS+ was 709 msec.
source: It was therefore surprising to observe that the median latency to ingress to the CS+ was 709 msec, and 27% of conditioned respones (CRs) were initiated at latencies higher than 1 s following CS+ onset (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Figure 6A shows the distribution of ingress onset latency during CS+ trials.

claim: 27% of conditioned responses were initiated at latencies higher than 1 s following CS+ onset.
source: It was therefore surprising to observe that the median latency to ingress to the CS+ was 709 msec, and 27% of conditioned respones (CRs) were initiated at latencies higher than 1 s following CS+ onset (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Figure 6A and 6B show the distribution and trial-by-trial latencies of ingress responses.

claim: The frequency of high-latency (>1 s) responses increased significantly as a function of trial number, from 4.2% on the first three trials to 39% on last three trials.
source: Precise measurement of CR onset revealed a second unanticipated feature: the frequency of high-latency (>1 s) responses increased significantly as a function of trial number, from 4.2% on the first three trials to 39% on last three trials (Figure 6C).
evidence: Figure 6C shows the percentage of high-latency ingresses increasing across trials with Spearman's correlation rs = 0.72, p=0.013.

claim: Extinction is characterized not only by a decrease in the probability of a CR but also by an increase in the latency to produce a CR.
source: Therefore, extinction is characterized not only by a decrease in the probability of a CR but also by an increase in the latency to produce a CR.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that high-latency responses increase with trial number during extinction (Figure 6C).

claim: The variance in mean firing rate accounted for by position, velocity and force is negligible (R2 = 9.3×10−3, 8.9 × 10−3, and 3.4 × 10−3, respectively).
source: Indeed, the variance in mean firing rate accounted for by position, velocity and force is negligible (Figure 7B, top; linear regression R2 = 9.3×10−3, 8.9 × 10−3, and 3.4 × 10−3, respectively).
evidence: Figure 7B shows the relationship between mean firing rate and behavioral variables with very low R2 values.

claim: At the single-unit level, the variance in firing rate accounted for by position, velocity and force is negligible (median R2 = 3.0×10−4, 1.8 × 10−3, and 1.1 × 10−3, respectively).
source: This observation also holds at the single-unit level (Figure 7B, bottom; linear regression median R2 = 3.0×10−4, 1.8 × 10−3, and 1.1 × 10−3, respectively).
evidence: Figure 7B bottom panel shows the distribution of R2 values for individual units.

claim: Behavior in the VBA does not sufficiently disrupt simultaneous neurophysiological recording as to prevent or cause spurious detection of spike waveforms.
source: We conclude that behavior in the VBA does not sufficiently disrupt simultaneous neurophysiological recording as to prevent or cause spurious detection of spike waveforms.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that firing rates are not significantly affected by behavioral variables (Figure 7).

claim: The VBA permits stable measurement of calcium transients in response to odorant stimuli using 2-photon microscopy through a GRIN lens implanted in the basolateral amygdala.
source: The assay also permits stable measurement of calcium transients in response to odorant stimuli using 2-photon microscopy through a GRIN lens implanted in the basolateral amygdala (O'Neill, P.K., personal communication).
evidence: This is stated based on personal communication, indicating unpublished data.

claim: The VBA reveals a diverse set of behavioral features related to sensory, cognitive, emotional and motor functions.
source: We have designed an assay for head-fixed mice that reveals a diverse set of behavioral features related to sensory, cognitive, emotional and motor functions.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates multiple behavioral features including sensory detection (Figures 2-4), discrimination (Figure 4), fear conditioning (Figure 5), and motor responses throughout.

claim: The VBA captures flight-like behavior.
source: The assay captures flight-like behavior (Figures 2 and 3), exploration (Figure 4), as well as the detection of the precise onset of conditioned responses to aversively conditioned odor stimuli (Figures 5 and 6)—measurements that have otherwise not been possible in head-fixed mice.
evidence: Figures 2 and 3 demonstrate rapid ingress responses to aversive stimuli interpreted as flight-like behavior.

claim: The VBA captures exploration behavior.
source: The assay captures flight-like behavior (Figures 2 and 3), exploration (Figure 4), as well as the detection of the precise onset of conditioned responses to aversively conditioned odor stimuli (Figures 5 and 6)—measurements that have otherwise not been possible in head-fixed mice.
evidence: Figure 4E-H demonstrates egress behavior interpreted as exploration when odor port is coupled to burrow.

claim: The VBA permits detection of the precise onset of conditioned responses to aversively conditioned odor stimuli.
source: The assay captures flight-like behavior (Figures 2 and 3), exploration (Figure 4), as well as the detection of the precise onset of conditioned responses to aversively conditioned odor stimuli (Figures 5 and 6)—measurements that have otherwise not been possible in head-fixed mice.
evidence: Figures 5 and 6 demonstrate precise measurement of conditioned response onset with millisecond resolution.

claim: These measurements have otherwise not been possible in head-fixed mice.
source: The assay captures flight-like behavior (Figures 2 and 3), exploration (Figure 4), as well as the detection of the precise onset of conditioned responses to aversively conditioned odor stimuli (Figures 5 and 6)—measurements that have otherwise not been possible in head-fixed mice.
evidence: This claim is made in the Discussion section, contrasting the VBA with existing head-fixed assays.

claim: The training-free approach may reduce variability due to differences in task proficiency across animals.
source: In contrast to standard training-based assays for head-fixed mice, this training-free approach may reduce variability due to differences in task proficiency across animals and minimize the complexity of the circuit operations necessary to produce meaningful behavior under head fixation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential advantages of the training-free approach.

claim: The training-free approach may minimize the complexity of the circuit operations necessary to produce meaningful behavior under head fixation.
source: In contrast to standard training-based assays for head-fixed mice, this training-free approach may reduce variability due to differences in task proficiency across animals and minimize the complexity of the circuit operations necessary to produce meaningful behavior under head fixation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential advantages of the training-free approach.

claim: The VBA measures behavior at a timescale comparable to that of neuronal dynamics.
source: Because it measures behavior at a timescale comparable to that of neuronal dynamics, the assay permits direct comparison between these two quantities.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates millisecond-scale behavioral measurements (e.g., Figure 2B showing ~18.5 msec latencies) comparable to neural timescales.

claim: Four observations suggest that ingress in the VBA reflects an innate behavioral program to seek the safety of an enclosure.
source: Four observations suggest that ingress in the VBA reflects an innate behavioral program to seek the safety of an enclosure.
evidence: The Discussion section lists four observations supporting this interpretation.

claim: Mice exhibit consistent and reliable ingress without training or even acclimation to head-fixation.
source: (1) Mice exhibit consistent and reliable ingress without training or even acclimation to head-fixation (Figure 1C) and invariably resist being pulled out of the burrow (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1C and 1D demonstrate these behaviors across N=10 mice.

claim: Mice invariably resist being pulled out of the burrow.
source: (1) Mice exhibit consistent and reliable ingress without training or even acclimation to head-fixation (Figure 1C) and invariably resist being pulled out of the burrow (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows force measurements demonstrating resistance across all mice tested.

claim: Ingress responses to air puff are characterized by markedly low latency and low variability across trials and across animals, indicative of a highly conserved behavior.
source: (2) Ingress responses to air puff are characterized by markedly low latency and low variability across trials and across animals (Figure 2A–C), indicative of a highly conserved behavior.
evidence: Figure 2B shows 15 consistent responses with mean latency of 18.5 msec and low coefficient of variation.

claim: Ingress does not depend upon the location of the source of the air puff but does require the availability of an enclosure.
source: (3) Ingress does not depend upon the location of the source of the air puff but does require the availability of an enclosure (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Figure 2D-F shows that mice ingress regardless of puff location (snout vs. hindquarters) in tube but not on platform.

claim: Mice ingress selectively to looming stimuli that evoke flight in freely moving mice.
source: (4) Mice ingress selectively to looming stimuli (Figure 3) that evoke flight in freely moving mice (De Franceschi et al., 2016; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: Figure 3 shows selective ingress to looming stimuli, and citations support that these stimuli evoke flight in freely moving mice.

claim: By simulating key features of the mouse Umwelt, the contingencies of the assay permit expression of innate behavioral programs in spite of the contrivance of the apparatus and of head-fixation.
source: We speculate that by simulating key features of the mouse Umwelt (von Uexküll, 1957), the contingencies of the assay permit expression of these innate behavioral programs in spite of the contrivance of the apparatus and of head-fixation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the assay successfully elicits innate behaviors.

claim: Four stimulus-induced behaviors have been observed in the VBA: flinch, ingress, egress bout, and trembling.
source: We have observed four stimulus-induced behaviors in this assay: flinch, ingress, egress bout, and trembling.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates all four behaviors in various figures throughout the Results section.

claim: Flinch in response to mild air puff is interpreted as a startle response.
source: We interpret flinch in response to mild air puff as a startle response (Davis, 1984); ingress in response to puff and looming stimuli as a flight-like response; egress bout as exploration; and trembling as a component of what is commonly referred to as 'freezing'.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to Davis, 1984 on startle responses.

claim: Ingress in response to puff and looming stimuli is interpreted as a flight-like response.
source: We interpret flinch in response to mild air puff as a startle response (Davis, 1984); ingress in response to puff and looming stimuli as a flight-like response; egress bout as exploration; and trembling as a component of what is commonly referred to as 'freezing'.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the rapid, stereotyped nature of the response and its similarity to flight behaviors.

claim: Egress bout is interpreted as exploration.
source: We interpret flinch in response to mild air puff as a startle response (Davis, 1984); ingress in response to puff and looming stimuli as a flight-like response; egress bout as exploration; and trembling as a component of what is commonly referred to as 'freezing'.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the observation that mice voluntarily egress to sample novel odors when the odor port is coupled to the burrow (Figure 4E-H).

claim: Trembling is interpreted as a component of what is commonly referred to as 'freezing'.
source: We interpret flinch in response to mild air puff as a startle response (Davis, 1984); ingress in response to puff and looming stimuli as a flight-like response; egress bout as exploration; and trembling as a component of what is commonly referred to as 'freezing'.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by observations of trembling in response to CS+ and similar observations in freely moving animals during fear conditioning.

claim: High-frequency trembling has been observed in wild rodents following the presentation of fear-inducing stimuli.
source: We made this same observation in high-speed video taken of freely moving animals during training in the conditioning chamber (data not shown), confirming previous reports of high-frequency trembling in wild rodents following the presentation fear-inducing stimuli (Griffith, 1920; Hofer, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Griffith, 1920 and Hofer, 1970, as well as unpublished video observations.

claim: When unanticipated stimuli were presented to mice in the exposed, egress position, they reliably ingressed.
source: When unanticipated stimuli were presented to mice in the exposed, egress position, they reliably ingressed (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Figure 4A-D shows ingress responses to novel odors when mice are in egress position.

claim: Mice briefly egressed in order to sample unanticipated stimuli if these were presented while the animals were ingressed.
source: In contrast, mice briefly egressed in order to sample unanticipated stimuli if these were presented while the animals were ingressed (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: Figure 4E-H shows egress responses to odors when mice start in ingress position with odor port coupled to burrow.

claim: The context-dependent response to unanticipated stimuli parallels the behavior of unconstrained animals, which exhibit either exploration (neophilia), avoidance (neophobia), or both in sequence, in a manner that depends on context.
source: This parallels the behavior of unconstrained animals, which exhibit either exploration (neophilia), avoidance (neophobia), or both in sequence, in a manner that depends on context (Berlyne, 1950; Gershman and Niv, 2015).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to literature on exploration and avoidance in freely moving animals.

claim: Many standard assays of rodent behavior in the laboratory measure events that unfold over seconds or minutes.
source: Many standard assays of rodent behavior in the laboratory measure events that unfold over seconds or minutes. These include time spent freezing (Bouton and Bolles, 1980; Griffith, 1920), conditioned suppression (Estes and Skinner, 1941), habituation (Groves and Thompson, 1970; Thompson and Spencer, 1966), approach versus avoidance (Young, 1959), conditioned place preference (Garcia et al., 1957), and exploration (Ennaceur and Delacour, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to standard behavioral assays.

claim: The VBA measures the onset of ingress and egress with millisecond precision.
source: The VBA measures the onset of ingress and egress with millisecond precision, thus permitting fine alignment of behavior with neural dynamics.
evidence: Figure 2B demonstrates millisecond-scale measurement of ingress onset (mean latency 18.5 msec).

claim: Alignment to sharp transitions in behavioral state has proven fruitful in primate neurophysiology.
source: Such alignment to sharp transitions in behavioral state has proven fruitful in primate neurophysiology: for instance, alignment to the precise time of eye saccades indicating a perceptual decision permits the investigation of the neuronal events underlying a decision process (Roitman and Shadlen, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roitman and Shadlen, 2002.

claim: The VBA can exploit stimulus-selective habituation to implement a discrimination assay without training.
source: The VBA can exploit stimulus-selective habituation to implement a discrimination assay without training.
evidence: Figure 4 demonstrates selective habituation to different odors, showing discrimination without training.

claim: Stimulus-selective habituation has been employed across many experimental systems, ranging from the olfactory system of freely moving rodents to the visual system of human infants.
source: This strategy has been employed across many experimental systems, ranging from the olfactory system of freely moving rodents (Cleland et al., 2002) to the visual system of human infants (Friedman, 1972), and can be exploited to construct psychometric curves for detection or discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cleland et al., 2002 and Friedman, 1972.

claim: Many head-fixed assays capable of measuring detection and discrimination depend upon instrumental conditioning, requiring acclimation to head-fixation and training in the sensorimotor contingencies of the task.
source: Many head-fixed assays are capable of measuring detection and discrimination (e.g. Guo et al., 2014), but these typically depend upon instrumental conditioning, requiring acclimation to head-fixation and training in the sensorimotor contingencies of the task; moreover, these are likely to result in perceptual learning (Fahle and Poggio, 2002), causing overestimation of default perceptual performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2014 and Fahle and Poggio, 2002.

claim: Training-based head-fixed assays are likely to result in perceptual learning, causing overestimation of default perceptual performance.
source: Many head-fixed assays are capable of measuring detection and discrimination (e.g. Guo et al., 2014), but these typically depend upon instrumental conditioning, requiring acclimation to head-fixation and training in the sensorimotor contingencies of the task; moreover, these are likely to result in perceptual learning (Fahle and Poggio, 2002), causing overestimation of default perceptual performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fahle and Poggio, 2002 on perceptual learning.

claim: Previously-described paradigms have successfully translated conditioned lick-suppression to a head-fixed preparation, but this measurement is characterized by relatively low temporal resolution.
source: Previously-described paradigms (such as Lovett-Barron et al., 2014) have successfully translated conditioned lick-suppression (Bouton and Bolles, 1980) to a head-fixed preparation, but this measurement is characterized by relatively low temporal resolution both in freely moving and in head-fixed mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lovett-Barron et al., 2014 and Bouton and Bolles, 1980.

claim: The observed latencies of conditioned ingress responses cannot be explained in terms of delays in sensory detection or ingress motor pattern generation.
source: These latencies cannot be explained in terms of delays in sensory detection (Resulaj and Rinberg, 2015) or ingress motor pattern generation (Figure 2).
evidence: This inference is based on comparing the long latencies observed in conditioning (median 709 msec) with rapid sensory detection (~100 msec from Resulaj and Rinberg, 2015) and rapid motor execution (~18.5 msec from Figure 2).

claim: A circuit centered around the amygdala has been proposed to orchestrate Pavlovian learning and the resultant expression of conditioned responses.
source: A circuit centered around the amygdala has been proposed to orchestrate Pavlovian learning and the resultant expression of conditioned responses (Johansen et al., 2011), but these results suggest that the expression of Pavlovian fear conditioning engages additional processing not accounted for in this model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johansen et al., 2011.

claim: The expression of Pavlovian fear conditioning engages additional processing not accounted for in the amygdala-centered model.
source: A circuit centered around the amygdala has been proposed to orchestrate Pavlovian learning and the resultant expression of conditioned responses (Johansen et al., 2011), but these results suggest that the expression of Pavlovian fear conditioning engages additional processing not accounted for in this model.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation of long and variable latencies in conditioned responses that cannot be explained by the simple amygdala-centered model.

claim: The wide range of responses measurable by the VBA yields sensitive indicators of sensory detection and discrimination thresholds, exploration, neophobia, memory, and motor function.
source: The wide range of responses measurable by the VBA yields sensitive indicators of sensory detection and discrimination thresholds, exploration, neophobia, memory, and motor function—behavioral features that may be affected in models of psychiatric and neurological diseases.
evidence: This claim summarizes the various behavioral measurements demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Animals habituate to odorant stimuli more rapidly when administered anxiolytics.
source: For example, in preliminary experiments we have found that animals habituate to odorant stimuli more rapidly when administered anxiolytics; and moreover, we have observed that the rate at which chronically stressed mice acclimate to the closed loop contingencies is diminished by the administration of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
evidence: This is described as a preliminary observation from unpublished experiments.

claim: The rate at which chronically stressed mice acclimate to the closed loop contingencies is diminished by the administration of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
source: For example, in preliminary experiments we have found that animals habituate to odorant stimuli more rapidly when administered anxiolytics; and moreover, we have observed that the rate at which chronically stressed mice acclimate to the closed loop contingencies is diminished by the administration of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
evidence: This is described as a preliminary observation from unpublished experiments.

claim: Key features of motor function—including balance, tremor, chorea, limb and core strength, movement initiation, and movement velocity—can be precisely measured by tracking the position of the burrow and the force exerted against the tether.
source: Moreover, key features of motor function—including balance, tremor, chorea, limb and core strength, movement initiation, and movement velocity—can be precisely measured by tracking the position of the burrow and the force exerted against the tether.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications based on the measurements the VBA can make.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocols AC-AAAI8650 and AC-AAAT5466).
source: All procedures were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocols AC-AAAI8650 and AC-AAAT5466).
evidence: This is a statement of ethical approval for the research.

claim: 8–17 week old, male C57BL/6J mice were used in the experiments.
source: 8–17 week old, male C57BL/6J mice (Jackson laboratories, Bar Harbor, ME) were fitted with a titanium head plate (27.4 mm x 9.0 mm x 0.8 mm, G. Johnson, Columbia University).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: Mice were allowed at least one full week and typically greater than 4 weeks to recover before any testing was performed.
source: Mice were allowed at least one full week and typically greater than 4 weeks to recover before any testing was performed (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the recovery period after surgery, with details in Table 1.

claim: All animals were singly housed on a 12 hr/12 hr light/dark cycle and were tested during their dark phase.
source: All animals were singly housed on a 12 hr/12 hr light/dark cycle and were tested during their dark phase.
evidence: This describes the housing and testing conditions for the animals.

claim: The VBA consists of a tube enclosure (virtual burrow), constrained to slide back and forth along the anterior-posterior axis of the body of a head-fixed mouse.
source: The VBA consists of a tube enclosure (virtual burrow), constrained to slide back and forth along the anterior-posterior axis of the body of a head-fixed mouse (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Figure 1A and 1B show diagrams and photographs of the VBA apparatus.

claim: The virtual burrow is coupled to near-frictionless air bushings at 14 psi input pressure.
source: The virtual burrow is coupled to near-frictionless air bushings at 14 psi input pressure (New Way Air Bearings, Aston, PA), which slide along two rails in order to constrain movement to one dimension (rail design and assembly: T. Tabachnik, ZMBBI Advanced Instrumentation, Columbia University: fabrication: Ronal Tool Company, Inc., York, PA) (Figure 1A, right and Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the mechanical design of the VBA apparatus.

claim: A laser displacement sensor measures the linear displacement of the tube along its axis of motion.
source: A laser displacement sensor (Part number: ILD1302-50, Micro-Epsilon, Dorfbach, Germany) is aimed at a flag affixed to the horizontal bar that joins the air bearings in order to measure the linear displacement of the tube along its axis of motion.
evidence: This describes the measurement system used in the VBA.

claim: The readout of the laser displacement sensor yields a continuous, time-dependent, one-dimensional variable that tracks ingress.
source: The readout of the laser displacement sensor yields a continuous, time-dependent, one-dimensional variable. It is this quantity – how far the animal has pulled the virtual burrow around its body – that tracks ingress in response to a given cue.
evidence: This describes what the laser displacement sensor measures and how it relates to behavior.

claim: The analog voltage signals from the laser displacement sensor and the force meter were acquired and digitized at 10 kHz.
source: For all experiments reported here the analog voltage signals from the laser displacement sensor and the force meter were acquired and digitized at 10 kHz using a Cerebus Neural Signal Processor (Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT).
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: Naïve mice maintain the burrow in the ingress position throughout a 2-10 minute acclimation period in open loop mode.
source: Prior to testing, naïve mice are head-fixed in the VBA and given 2–10 mn to acclimate to the contingencies in open loop (free movement of the burrow). Without exception, mice maintain the burrow in the ingress position throughout this acclimation period (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the consistent behavior observed during acclimation, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Mice do not require more than ~5 minutes total acclimation time (typically two minutes for open loop and ~3 minutes for closed loop).
source: The duration of the closed-loop acclimation period varied across mice in these experiments (1–20 mn) as the experimenters improved upon and acquired experience withthe assay; presently mice do not require more than ~5 mn total acclimation time (typically two mn for open loop and ~3 mn for closed loop).
evidence: This describes the optimized acclimation protocol developed over the course of the experiments.

claim: We have not observed any mice that fail to resist retraction of the virtual burrow.
source: We have not observed any mice that fail to resist retraction of the virtual burrow.
evidence: This is a statement about the universality of the resistance behavior across all tested animals.

claim: The probability of ingress to looming stimulus was significantly different from receding stimulus (p=1.5×10−05).
source: A two-proportion z-test pooled across all mice (N = 3) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differs significantly across stimulus conditions. p(loom,recede)=1.5×10−05, p(loom,sweep)=4.6×10−04, p(recede,sweep)=0.072.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the visual stimulus experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The probability of ingress to looming stimulus was significantly different from sweeping stimulus (p=4.6×10−04).
source: A two-proportion z-test pooled across all mice (N = 3) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differs significantly across stimulus conditions. p(loom,recede)=1.5×10−05, p(loom,sweep)=4.6×10−04, p(recede,sweep)=0.072.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the visual stimulus experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The probability of ingress to receding stimulus was not significantly different from sweeping stimulus (p=0.072).
source: A two-proportion z-test pooled across all mice (N = 3) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differs significantly across stimulus conditions. p(loom,recede)=1.5×10−05, p(loom,sweep)=4.6×10−04, p(recede,sweep)=0.072.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the visual stimulus experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The probability of ingress differed significantly between the first three presentations of Odor 1 and all subsequent presentations (p=8.8×10−10).
source: A two-proportion z-test on ingress probability pooled across all mice (N = 5) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differed significantly between the first three presentations of each odorant stimulus and all subsequent presentations of that odorant; ingress defined as maximum displacement >2 mm during the 8 s stimulus epoch, indicated by the dashed line. p(Odor1 trials 1–3, Odor1 trials 4–45)=8.8×10−10, p(Odor2 trials 1–3, Odor2 trials 4–30)=1.9×10−04, p(Odor3 trials 1–3, Odor3 trials 4–15)=2.2×10−06.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the habituation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The probability of ingress differed significantly between the first three presentations of Odor 2 and all subsequent presentations (p=1.9×10−04).
source: A two-proportion z-test on ingress probability pooled across all mice (N = 5) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differed significantly between the first three presentations of each odorant stimulus and all subsequent presentations of that odorant; ingress defined as maximum displacement >2 mm during the 8 s stimulus epoch, indicated by the dashed line. p(Odor1 trials 1–3, Odor1 trials 4–45)=8.8×10−10, p(Odor2 trials 1–3, Odor2 trials 4–30)=1.9×10−04, p(Odor3 trials 1–3, Odor3 trials 4–15)=2.2×10−06.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the habituation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The probability of ingress differed significantly between the first three presentations of Odor 3 and all subsequent presentations (p=2.2×10−06).
source: A two-proportion z-test on ingress probability pooled across all mice (N = 5) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differed significantly between the first three presentations of each odorant stimulus and all subsequent presentations of that odorant; ingress defined as maximum displacement >2 mm during the 8 s stimulus epoch, indicated by the dashed line. p(Odor1 trials 1–3, Odor1 trials 4–45)=8.8×10−10, p(Odor2 trials 1–3, Odor2 trials 4–30)=1.9×10−04, p(Odor3 trials 1–3, Odor3 trials 4–15)=2.2×10−06.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the habituation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The maximum change in burrow position during exploration differed significantly between trials 1-2 and trials 3-5 (p=0.0021).
source: A Wilcoxon rank-sum test was employed to evaluate whether the maximum change in burrow position differed significantly (p(trials1-2,trials3-5)=0.0021, N = 5 mice).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the exploration experiments shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The probability of ingress to CS+ was significantly different from CS- during Test (p=1.0×10−05).
source: A two-proportion z-test on ingress probability on trials 2–7 (6 trials per mouse, pooled across N = 9 mice) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differed significantly; statistical analysis was restricted to trials 2–7 to mitigate the effects of recovery observed on the first trial and extinction observed on the last four trials; ingress defined as maximum displacement >2 mm during the 8 s stimulus. p(CS+,CS-)=1.0×10−05, p(CS+,O3)=5.0×10−05, p(CS-,O3)=0.35.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fear conditioning experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The probability of ingress to CS+ was significantly different from Odor3 during Test (p=5.0×10−05).
source: A two-proportion z-test on ingress probability on trials 2–7 (6 trials per mouse, pooled across N = 9 mice) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differed significantly; statistical analysis was restricted to trials 2–7 to mitigate the effects of recovery observed on the first trial and extinction observed on the last four trials; ingress defined as maximum displacement >2 mm during the 8 s stimulus. p(CS+,CS-)=1.0×10−05, p(CS+,O3)=5.0×10−05, p(CS-,O3)=0.35.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fear conditioning experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The probability of ingress to CS- was not significantly different from Odor3 during Test (p=0.35).
source: A two-proportion z-test on ingress probability on trials 2–7 (6 trials per mouse, pooled across N = 9 mice) was employed to evaluate whether the probability of ingress differed significantly; statistical analysis was restricted to trials 2–7 to mitigate the effects of recovery observed on the first trial and extinction observed on the last four trials; ingress defined as maximum displacement >2 mm during the 8 s stimulus. p(CS+,CS-)=1.0×10−05, p(CS+,O3)=5.0×10−05, p(CS-,O3)=0.35.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fear conditioning experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The statistical result for CS+ vs CS- discrimination is robust to the choice of ingress threshold over a range of 0.5 to 10 mm.
source: This result is robust to the choice of ingress threshold over a range of 0.5 to 10 mm (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2 shows the p-values remain below 0.05 across a range of thresholds.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the fraction of high-latency ingress and trial number (rs = 0.72, p=0.013).
source: The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was computed to measure the strength of the relationship between the fraction of high-latency ingress and trial number (rs = 0.72, p=0.013).
evidence: This statistical result is shown in Figure 6C demonstrating increasing latencies during extinction.

claim: Mice can report discrimination of odor stimuli within ~100 msec.
source: Mice can report discrimination of odor stimuli within ~100 msec (Resulaj and Rinberg, 2015) and we have demonstrated that they are capable of initiating stimulus-evoked ingress within ~20 msec (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Resulaj and Rinberg, 2015.
